questions.stem: Which property increases steadily going down Group 7?

options.text: Melting point
options.explanation: Heavier halogens need more heat to overcome stronger intermolecular attractions, so their melting points climb.

options.text: Volatility
options.explanation: Higher boiling points mean evaporation happens less readily, so volatility falls rather than rises.

options.text: Electronegativity
options.explanation: Larger atoms attract bonding electrons more weakly, so electronegativity drops down the group.

options.text: Reactivity
options.explanation: Bigger atoms hold incoming electrons less strongly, so reactivity as oxidising agents falls.

questions.stem: Why does iodine evaporate far less readily than fluorine?

options.text: Iodine has a higher electronegativity that traps its electrons
options.explanation: Electronegativity decreases down the group, and it governs electron attraction in bonds, not evaporation.

options.text: Its diatomic molecules have many more electrons, strengthening the induced dipole-dipole attractions between them
options.explanation: More electrons per molecule means stronger London dispersion forces that must be supplied with heat to vaporise.

options.text: Iodine forms covalent networks that need breaking before it melts
options.explanation: Iodine is simple molecular, not a giant network, so no covalent lattice is disrupted on evaporation.

options.text: Iodine molecules are lighter and move more slowly
options.explanation: Iodine molecules are heavier, not lighter, and mass is not the direct cause here.

questions.stem: A volatile substance is best described as one that

options.text: Has strong forces inside its covalent molecules
options.explanation: Volatility depends on forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them.

options.text: Conducts electricity when molten
options.explanation: That is a property of ionic or metallic substances, irrelevant to volatility.

options.text: Evaporates easily because it boils at a low temperature
options.explanation: Volatility describes ease of evaporation, which tracks a low boiling point.

options.text: Reacts vigorously with water to give an acid
options.explanation: That describes reactivity with water, not volatility.

questions.stem: Which set orders halogen colour correctly going down the group?

options.text: Dark iodine, red-brown bromine, green chlorine, pale fluorine
options.explanation: That lists the group upwards, the reverse of the asked direction.

options.text: Green fluorine, yellow chlorine, orange bromine, silver iodine
options.explanation: These shades misassign the well-known halogen colours.

options.text: All halogens are colourless gases at room temperature
options.explanation: Halogens have distinct colours, and bromine is a liquid, iodine a solid.

options.text: Pale yellow fluorine, yellow-green chlorine, red-brown bromine, dark grey-black iodine
options.explanation: The colours darken progressively from fluorine to iodine in this order.

questions.stem: Bromine is used in flame retardants. Its room-temperature state and volatility compared with chlorine are

options.text: Liquid, and less volatile because its molecules attract each other more strongly
options.explanation: Bromine sits below chlorine, so its molecules carry more electrons, attract each other more, and it is the liquid halogen.

options.text: Gas, and more volatile because it is heavier
options.explanation: Bromine is a liquid at room temperature and heavier molecules are less volatile, not more.

options.text: Solid, and more volatile because it is dark coloured
options.explanation: Colour depth does not create volatility, and bromine is not solid.

options.text: Liquid, and more volatile because dark colours absorb heat
options.explanation: Absorbed colour has nothing to do with volatility; the intermolecular attraction decides it.

questions.stem: Define volatility.
questions.modelAnswer: Volatility is how easily a substance evaporates; a volatile substance has a low boiling point.

questions.stem: State the trend in halogen colours down Group 7.
questions.modelAnswer: The colours get darker going down the group, from pale fluorine through green chlorine and red-brown bromine to dark iodine.

questions.stem: Explain why boiling points of the halogens rise down the group.
questions.modelAnswer: Descending the group each diatomic molecule carries more electrons, so instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between the simple molecular halogens strengthen, and more energy is needed to separate the molecules into gas.

questions.stem: A student spills liquid bromine and it soon fumes but the iodine crystals beside it barely change. Account for both observations.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine, with more electrons per molecule than chlorine but fewer than iodine, sits mid-ladder: volatile enough to fume at room temperature, while iodine's far stronger intermolecular attractions hold its molecules in the solid, so it sublimes only slowly.

questions.stem: What structure do the halogens adopt at room temperature?

options.text: Metallic lattices with delocalised electrons
options.explanation: Halogens are non-metals; there are no delocalised electrons to carry charge.

options.text: Simple molecular, as diatomic molecules with weak forces between the molecules
options.explanation: Halogen pairs are held covalently inside but only by induced dipole-induced dipole forces outside, the simple molecular pattern.

options.text: Giant covalent lattices of linked atoms
options.explanation: No covalent network joins different halogen molecules; each exists as a two-atom unit.

options.text: Giant ionic lattices of halide ions
options.explanation: The elements are neutral molecules, not ion arrays; halide ions appear in their compounds.

questions.stem: Electronegativity falls down Group 7 mainly because

options.text: The molecules become diatomic and share electrons internally
options.explanation: Diatomicity is constant across the group and does not set electronegativity.

options.text: Electronegativity is constant because all halogens need one electron
options.explanation: The group shares valency, but electronegativity still varies with size.

options.text: Atomic radius and shielding increase, so the outer shell feels less nuclear attraction
options.explanation: Larger atoms hold their bonding electrons more weakly as distance and inner-shell screening grow.

options.text: Nuclear charge decreases as you go down the group
options.explanation: Nuclear charge actually rises with proton number; shielding outweighs it.

questions.stem: Which statement about oxidising power of the halogens is correct?

options.text: It increases down the group as atoms get heavier
options.explanation: Extra mass does not help electron capture; the pull weakens.

options.text: It stays constant because each halogen forms a 1- ion
options.explanation: Forming the same charge does not mean the same ease of gaining electrons.

options.text: It depends only on the melting point of the halogen
options.explanation: Melting point tracks intermolecular force, not electron capture.

options.text: It decreases down the group, matching the fall in electronegativity
options.explanation: A weaker pull on incoming electrons makes each heavier halogen a poorer oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Why are the melting points of the halogens low compared with ionic substances?

options.text: Only weak induced dipole-induced dipole forces between molecules need overcoming
options.explanation: Melting separates whole molecules, so the weak intermolecular attractions set the low energy cost.

options.text: Covalent bonds inside each diatomic molecule are weak
options.explanation: The covalent X-X bonds are strong; melting never breaks them.

options.text: The molecules carry permanent charges that repel
options.explanation: Halogen molecules are neutral with only fleeting dipoles.

options.text: Halogen molecules cannot pack closely together
options.explanation: Packing is not the issue; the attraction strength is.

questions.stem: An instantaneous dipole-induced dipole force arises when

options.text: Electrons are transferred completely between the two molecules
options.explanation: Full transfer is ionic bonding, not an intermolecular attraction.

options.text: A fleeting electron imbalance in one molecule induces a matching dipole in its neighbour
options.explanation: A momentary unequal electron distribution creates a dipole that polarises the nearby molecule, and the two attract.

options.text: A permanent dipole in one molecule aligns with another permanent dipole
options.explanation: That describes permanent dipole-dipole forces, not the induced type.

options.text: A hydrogen atom bridges two electronegative atoms
options.explanation: That is hydrogen bonding, a different intermolecular force.

questions.stem: Define electronegativity.
questions.modelAnswer: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond.

questions.stem: State and explain the trend in oxidising power down Group 7.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidising power decreases down the group because atoms get larger, outer electrons sit further from the nucleus with more shielding, and the pull on an incoming electron weakens.

questions.stem: Explain why fluorine is the most electronegative halogen.
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so its bonding electrons in a covalent bond, or an incoming electron, feel the least shielding and the shortest distance to a strongly positive nucleus, giving the strongest attraction.

questions.stem: Predict, with reasons, whether astatine below iodine would be a stronger or weaker oxidising agent than iodine.
questions.modelAnswer: Weaker: astatine atoms are larger still, so incoming electrons meet even more shielding and greater distance from the nucleus, reducing the pull that makes a halogen an oxidising agent.

questions.stem: When chlorine reacts to form chloride, the oxidation number change is

options.text: 0 to +1, so chlorine is oxidised
options.explanation: Chlorine gains electrons here; it does not lose them to become positive.

options.text: +7 to -1, a seven-electron gain
options.explanation: That leap belongs to chlorine in oxyanions like chlorate(VII), not to the free element.

options.text: 0 to -1, so chlorine is reduced
options.explanation: The neutral atom gains one electron, dropping its oxidation number by one unit into the halide.

options.text: -1 to 0, so chlorine is oxidised
options.explanation: That reverses the actual electron flow during halide formation.

questions.stem: Why does iodine react less vigorously than chlorine with metals?

options.text: Iodine molecules contain stronger covalent bonds that resist breaking
options.explanation: I-I is actually the weakest halogen-halogen bond; electron capture, not bond strength, limits reactivity.

options.text: Iodine has a smaller nuclear charge than chlorine
options.explanation: Iodine's nucleus is much more positively charged; shielding is what weakens the pull.

options.text: Iodide ions repel metal ions more strongly
options.explanation: Repulsion between products is not the mechanism of the trend.

options.text: Its larger atoms shield and distance the incoming electron from the nucleus, weakening the attraction
options.explanation: Poorer electron capture means weaker oxidising power and slower, less vigorous reactions.

questions.stem: In the reaction of a halogen with hydrogen gas, the halogen acts as

options.text: An oxidising agent, because hydrogen's oxidation number rises from 0 to +1
options.explanation: The halogen takes hydrogen's electron, being reduced itself while oxidising hydrogen.

options.text: A reducing agent, because it donates electrons to hydrogen
options.explanation: The electron flow is towards the halogen, not away from it.

options.text: A catalyst, because it speeds hydrogen splitting without change
options.explanation: The halogen is consumed into the hydrogen halide product.

options.text: A spectator, because its oxidation number never changes
options.explanation: The halogen's oxidation number falls from 0 to -1.

questions.stem: The reaction with hydrogen provides evidence for the reactivity trend because

options.text: Hydrogen oxidises each halogen in turn
options.explanation: The halogen is the oxidising agent in these reactions.

options.text: The vigour of the reaction with hydrogen decreases steadily down the group
options.explanation: A visibly gentler reaction with each heavier halogen demonstrates the falling oxidising power.

options.text: All halogens react with hydrogen at identical rates
options.explanation: The whole point of the test is the graded vigour down the group.

options.text: Hydrogen chloride is the only product any halogen forms
options.explanation: Each halogen forms its own hydrogen halide HX.

questions.stem: Which half-equation matches the electron gain that turns a halogen atom into a halide?

options.explanation: That loses electrons, the opposite of halogen reduction.
The product is two separate bromide ions, not a doubly charged molecule.
Each of the two atoms gains one electron, so the molecule needs two electrons to form two bromides.

options.text: Br2 + e- -> Br2-
options.explanation: A single electron cannot convert the whole molecule; each atom takes one.

questions.stem: State what happens to the oxidation number of a halogen when it reacts to form its halide ion.
questions.modelAnswer: It falls from 0 to -1 as the atom gains one electron, so reduction has occurred.

questions.stem: Explain why fluorine reacts more vigorously with hydrogen than iodine does.
questions.modelAnswer: Fluorine attracts the incoming electron far more strongly because of its small size and low shielding, so its oxidising power and reaction vigour are greater than iodine's.

questions.stem: Explain why halogens act as oxidising agents in reactions with metals.
questions.modelAnswer: The halogen atom gains the electrons that the metal loses, so the halogen is reduced while oxidising the metal, which is the defining action of an oxidising agent.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts far more violently with chlorine than with iodine. Predict the comparable vigour with bromine and justify the ordering.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine should sit between them: it oxidises sodium more readily than iodine but less readily than chlorine, because its electron capture is intermediate - larger than chlorine's yet stronger than iodine's.
